title: Experiment 2: duplicate orders
content:
← Section contents
Identical messages for dup-proof-20261113-220937-a7468d were submitted to SQS five times. Results: execution SUCCEEDED, one successful SES task in that execution, DynamoDB DONE, and emailCount = 1.
Logs show duplicates being skipped. Two workflow-started log lines do not establish two executions: Standard StartExecution with the same name and input can return an existing running execution.
Logs showing duplicate orders skipped
The inbox received a confirmation with the matching order ID. These observations support duplicate handling in this test, not guaranteed exactly-once email delivery under all failures.
Received confirmation email
Replay one purchase with a stable identity The recorded trial submitted one body directly to SQS five times. This exercises the downstream worker and workflow. The intake API is outside this particular test. For a repeat, choose a verified test inbox to observe email delivery or the simulator to observe only SES task success. Keep the ID and business payload identical across the sends. A new random ID each time would be a different experiment.
$q = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='QueueUrl'].OutputValue | [0]" --region ap-southeast-1 --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or $q -eq 'None') { throw 'QueueUrl unavailable.' } $dupId = 'dup-' + [guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N').Substring(0,10) $email = Read-Host 'Verified test recipient (Enter = SES simulator)' if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($email)) { $email = 'success@simulator.amazonses.com' } $body = @{ orderId = $dupId; customerEmail = $email } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress $file = Join-Path $PWD.Path "$dupId.json" [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $body, [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) 1..5 | ForEach-Object { aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body "file://$file" --region ap-southeast-1 --query MessageId --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Send $_ failed." } } $dupId Each accepted send returns a message ID. Five submissions describe one purchase. Locate the execution named for $dupId and count successful SES tasks in its history. Then inspect status and emailCount under the same table key. For a real inbox, find the subject containing the fresh ID. Reading results requires no sixth submission.
Investigate counts that disagree For two “started” log lines, count distinct execution ARNs first. For one execution with multiple successful SES tasks, inspect state history, timing and retries. For a single item with a counter greater than one, verify the template version and run ID. Each observation narrows the next investigation. Report actual mailbox count only when you have inspected that inbox.

title: Troubleshooting
content:
← Section contents
Lambda does not run: go to Console → Lambda → the ProcessOrderFn function → Configuration → Triggers tab, and check that the SQS trigger is Enabled. DynamoDB permission error: check the log, and make sure the Policies section of the template uses the correct !Ref OrdersTable. sam logs shows nothing: wait a few seconds and send the message again, as logs have a small delay. Narrow the search from queue to table Start with a fresh order ID and a UTC send time. Confirm that SQS returned a message ID. Then look for an invocation of the intended function in the same interval. Visible messages with an inactive mapping point to the trigger. A fall in visible count with an increase in in-flight messages can mean processing is underway or a failed delivery is waiting for its visibility timeout.
sam logs --stack-name order-system --name ProcessOrderFn --region ap-southeast-1 --start-time '15min ago' Look for the ID or the first exception near its send time. For Runtime.ImportModuleError inspect the handler file, CodeUri and packaged dependencies. For denied PutItem access check the execution role and table ARN. A handled conditional write failure is expected for a duplicate. Keep the time alongside the observation because one stream can contain many orders.
Verify a correction with a small case Change one factor at a time. Rebuild and update the same stack after a code or template edit. Changing a log filter only requires reading the log again. To recheck new-order processing, use a fresh ID. To test the duplicate branch, intentionally reuse the ID. Record the original symptom, change made and observed outcome. These three lines document a reproducible repair.

title: Troubleshooting
content:
← Section contents
Not receiving the order confirmation email: check that both SenderEmail and the customer email are Verified in SES, and check your spam folder. Not receiving the alert: check whether you clicked Confirm subscription in SNS (Console → SNS → Subscriptions, the status must be Confirmed). No execution at all: check the ProcessOrderFn logs; if there is a permissions error, review the Policies section in the template. Execution reports an AccessDenied error at SES: check that the state machine’s role has ses:SendEmail. Trace the symptom to the responsible service For a missing confirmation, start with the customer’s order ID. A missing item leads back to the queue and worker. A RECEIVED item leads to the execution name. Once an execution is found, inspect the final state reached and the first failure. This sequence avoids changing SES verification when the worker has not yet started the state machine.
If the SES task reports access denied, inspect the state machine role and the allowed action. If SES reports an unverified identity, check the sender, test recipient and Region. For rate limiting after a burst, read retry history before submitting again manually. A manual resend adds another request to the experiment and can obscure the original cause.
Investigate FAILED with no administrative email Find NotifyAdminFailure in execution history. If it was never reached, inspect the preceding table update. For a denied publish, identify the role and topic ARN from the error. For a successful publish, check the confirmed subscription, inbox and spam folder of the intended administrative address. Record the last confirmed step before attributing the incident.
After the correction, use a fresh test order. Keep the old execution as a reference for comparison. The old ID, new ID and single change between runs document the repair.

title: Experiment 3: failures and alerts
content:
← Section contents
SES failure and retries Order failure-proof-20261113-222244-4343a2 used not-an-email. SES returned SesV2.BadRequestException, HTTP 400, cause Missing final ‘@domain’. Event history shows task rescheduling and execution after failures. SDK Attempt Count: 1 is not the total Step Functions retry count.
Failure branch Catch routed to MarkFailed and NotifyAdminFailure, both successful. The workflow terminated at OrderFailed; MarkDone was skipped.
Workflow failure-handling branch
The SNS email contains the matching order ID and was sent by NotifyAdminFailure.
Alert email from the workflow
DLQ and CloudWatch Alarm A separate test used invalid JSON: not-json-dlq-proof-20261113-223327-eed369. Inspect the message in order-orchestration-evidence-OrdersDLQ-Kbv9OO2FitbU; the screenshot should show both the queue name and message body.
Malformed message in the identified DLQ
Alarm order-orchestration-evidence-dlq-proof monitored the DLQ ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric and entered ALARM at November 13, 2026, 15:39:57 UTC.
Triggered DLQ alarm
The CloudWatch email delivered through SNS records the same alarm and transition time, with datapoint 1 exceeding threshold 0. This is distinct from the workflow notification above. These screenshots do not measure alert latency.
CloudWatch alarm email via SNS
Follow two distinct failure paths not-an-email is still a string inside valid JSON. The worker can record the order and start an execution before SES validates the address and rejects it. A not-json-... body fails at the worker parser and never reaches the email state. Keep separate markers so you do not search for a workflow execution that could never start.
$q = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='QueueUrl'].OutputValue | [0]" --region ap-southeast-1 --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or $q -eq 'None') { throw 'QueueUrl unavailable.' } $tag = [guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N').Substring(0,10) $failedId = "ses-fail-$tag" $badBody = "not-json-$tag" $file = Join-Path $PWD.Path "$failedId.json" $body = @{ orderId = $failedId; customerEmail = 'not-an-email' } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $body, [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)) aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body "file://$file" --region ap-southeast-1 --query MessageId --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'First send failed.' } aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body $badBody --region ap-southeast-1 --query MessageId --output text --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Second send failed.' } [pscustomobject]@{ OrderId = $failedId; DlqMarker = $badBody } For the first case, inspect the first error, task reschedules, table update and NotifyAdminFailure publish. The 5.7 template permits six retries, so allow for backoff before checking the terminal state. A recorded environment may have different retry settings. Count events for the run you actually inspect. For the second case, find $badBody in the application’s DLQ and check the corresponding alarm from 5.6.
Capture comparable timestamps Separating detection time and mail delivery needs the initial error from history or a log, the alarm transition and the inbox arrival. Convert all three to UTC before subtracting. The SNS notification timestamp describes a service event and may differ from mailbox receipt. If the DLQ was already in alarm, the new item can arrive without a new state-transition email. Record that as a valid observation of the configured alarm behavior.

title: Fault and Load Experiments
content:
Objective Compare two ways of processing orders under the same conditions:
Synchronous (baseline) Asynchronous (proposed) Flow The API writes to DynamoDB and then sends via SES within the request The API only puts the order into SQS; Lambda and Step Functions process it later Duplicate protection No Yes (DynamoDB) Retry, DLQ, alerts No Yes Metrics: API response time (average, p95), completed orders, failed or lost orders, processing completion time, extra emails when duplicates are sent, and the time until an alert is raised on failure.
SES sandbox limit: at most 1 email/second. Emails sent to success@simulator.amazonses.com (the SES mailbox simulator) do not count toward the 200 emails/day quota but are still limited to 1 email/second. That is why the test loads are 20 and 50 orders. This is also a result worth recording: the bottleneck is the email-sending service, not the architecture.

title: Resource cleanup
content:
Objective Delete all the resources you created so that no charges are incurred, especially the two public APIs from section 5.7.
Before deletion Save the 5.7 results and check the profile, Region and stack names. If you deployed the separate monitoring stack in 5.6.3, remove it first to retire alarms pointing at resources about to be deleted. Run the following block only for your dedicated order-monitoring lab stack.
$monitorStack = 'order-monitoring' aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name $monitorStack --region ap-southeast-1 --query 'Stacks[0].{Stack:StackName,Status:StackStatus}' --output table --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Check the monitoring stack name and Region.' } if ((Read-Host "Type $monitorStack to remove this lab monitoring stack") -ceq $monitorStack) { aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name $monitorStack --region ap-southeast-1 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Deletion request failed.' } aws cloudformation wait stack-delete-complete --stack-name $monitorStack --region ap-southeast-1 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Inspect stack events before continuing.' } } 1. Delete the main stack sam delete --stack-name order-system --region ap-southeast-1 Answer y to the confirmation prompts. This command deletes the CloudFormation stack together with SQS, the DLQ, DynamoDB, Lambda, Step Functions, SNS, other resources in this stack, and the HTTP API.
Check that the latest deployment of the stack is DELETE_COMPLETE. CloudFormation can retain earlier stack history.
aws cloudformation list-stacks --region ap-southeast-1 --query "StackSummaries[?StackName=='order-system'].[StackName,StackStatus,CreationTime]" --output table --no-cli-pager 2. Delete the Lambda log groups Lambda creates its log groups automatically, so they are not deleted with the stack:
$groups = aws logs describe-log-groups --region ap-southeast-1 --log-group-name-prefix '/aws/lambda/order-system-' --query 'logGroups[].logGroupName' --output json --no-cli-pager if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Cannot list log groups.' } foreach ($name in ($groups | Out-String | ConvertFrom-Json)) { if ((Read-Host "Type DELETE to remove the lab log group $name") -ceq 'DELETE') { aws logs delete-log-group --region ap-southeast-1 --log-group-name $name if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Could not delete $name." } } } 3. Delete the SAM managed stack (optional) Only remove SAM resources dedicated to this lab. SAM also creates the aws-sam-cli-managed-default stack along with an S3 bucket that holds the deployment code. The cost is very small, but you can clean it up: go to S3, open the bucket whose name starts with aws-sam-cli-managed-default, choose Empty, then go to CloudFormation and delete the aws-sam-cli-managed-default stack.
4. Delete the verified email in SES (optional) Go to Amazon SES → Identities → select the email → Delete.
5. Revoke access Do this step last, because once the key is deleted the CLI can no longer be used:
Go to IAM → Users → select the user → Security credentials → Deactivate and then Delete the access key. Detach the OrderWorkshopDeployPolicy policy from the user, then delete the policy if it is no longer needed. title: Conclusion
content:
← Section contents
Both modes reached DONE for 20/20 orders in this run. Separate tests recorded duplicate handling, SES retries, SNS failure notifications and DLQ alerts. Findings are limited to the documented test conditions and runs.
Choose the architecture using both timelines For a customer waiting at checkout, the relevant interval begins when the client sends the request and ends on intake confirmation. In the recorded run both groups had 20 successful HTTP responses. Client-side means were 229.55 ms for sync and 109.28 ms for async. The async storefront can immediately present the order ID and acceptance status. Reporting completion at that point would get ahead of the workflow.
For support staff checking progress, the relevant observation is the final DONE or FAILED for that ID. Approximate mean completion was 122.75 ms for sync and 445.55 ms for async in the measured groups. Those times come from application fields. Their relationship to client latency depends on clock boundaries and how much work continues outside the request. Treating them as interchangeable leads to incorrect status messages.
Link the conclusion to the experiment Experiment Recorded observation Scope Small API run 20/20 DONE for each mode at concurrency one Async intake responded faster in the recorded conditions Five sends of one body One verified execution, one successful SES task, counter one Duplicate handling worked for that ID and scenario Rejected email Error, retry and administrative path in history A failure after acceptance can be traced Malformed body Matching DLQ body and an observed alarm Failed input can be retained for investigation Incident notification latency Matching timestamp pair unavailable The interval remains unmeasured Include submitted requests, distinct order IDs, the observation time and actual sample count with a comparison. Treat a change of recipient type or worker concurrency as a new run. Retain the original population as a reference.
Hand over results before cleanup Choose one successful and one failed order you actually submitted. For each, record the API path or queue source, final state, evidence inspected and any open question. For invalid input lacking an order ID, use the body marker and DLQ name. Together with the latency table, these records let another reader check the reasoning without opening your AWS account.
Before section 5.8 removes resources, save the prefixes, benchmark output and final observation time. This matters for logs and items belonging to the stack that will be removed. Billing needs its own check for newly accrued charges. A configured budget or a small value on a single billing view does not supply that measurement.
Revisit the conclusion when the business requirement changes A merchant who needs only “request received” while the customer is at checkout can evaluate the first screen using API latency and a traceable order ID. The customer can check the final state afterward. If the success screen promises that the email was submitted and processing was recorded, the measurement must extend to completion. The recorded table supplies two distinct intervals for that decision.
Another requirement might give the operator a notification deadline. Received emails establish that a notification channel worked on the observed run. The missing timestamp of the initiating fault still prevents a fault-to-notification measurement. Name which requirement was exercised and which needs an additional observation. A later run can use the same resources while recording the original error time and correlating alarm history with the corresponding inbox message.
Write a result paragraph from a new run “Run … in Singapore used … distinct orders per mode at concurrency …. API mean/P95 were … for sync and … for async. At … UTC the table contained … DONE, … FAILED and … pending. Order … demonstrated the failure path at state …. The … measure lacks source or timestamp ….” Fill the fields from observations and leave unresolved fields open. This places conditions, measurements and limitations together for a fair comparison with the recorded run.
